newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says Indonesia policy not altered by money.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Indonesia policy not altered by money.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday denied that any contributions to the Democratic Party from an Indonesian businessman influenced U.S. policy toward Indonesia.
"The answer to that is absolutely not," Clinton told a news conference at which he was peppered with questions about questionable contributions to the Democratic Party.

Republicans have raised questions as to whether the family of Indonesian businessman James Riady, who has longstanding ties to Clinton, influenced U.S. policy toward Indonesia by contributing $475,000 to the Democratic Party and its candidates since 1991.

The Justice Department on Friday rejected a request by the citizen's lobbying group Common Cause for an independent counsel to investigate alleged violations of finance laws by both the Democratic and Republican presidential campaigns.

But Attorney General Janet Reno was still considering a separate request by five congressional Republicans for an independent counsel to investigate allegations that the Democrats engaged in illegal fund-raising activities.

It mainly involves allegations of illegal foreign contributions and the activities of Riady associate John Huang, a Democratic Pary fundraiser, who helped solicit large sums of money from Asian Americans.

Answering questions about the controversy for the first time since it broke a month ago, Clinton made a case that U.S. policy toward Indonesia had actually been tougher under his presidency than his predecessor George Bush.

He said America decided not to sell small arms to Indonesia because of questionable human rights practices in East Timor, a former Portuguese policy seeking independence from Indonesia. He said the United States also co-sponsored a U.N. resolution in favour of improved human rights for East Timor.
"I'm proud that we did that so I can tell you categorically that there was no influence," he said.

Questionable contributions from foreign nationals have forced John Huang, who worked for Clinton as an assistant secretary in the Commerce Department, to step down from his job as a top Democratic fund-raiser.

On Thursday, the Democratic National Committee announced it had decided to return a Huang-solicited $325,000 contribution from Yogesh Gandhi, a great-grandnephew of the late Indian spiritual leader Mohandas Gandhi, after it became clear he had no assets or bank accounts in the United States.

Clinton would not say whether he believed the Justice Department should heed Republican appeals to appoint an independent counsel to look into the matter, saying it was inappropriate for him to comment.
And he gave no vote of confidence to Reno in her quest to stay in her job in Clinton's second term.
"I should have no comment on any personnel decision until I have had a chance to meet with the Cabinet members in question and work through all the decisions," he said.
He repeated his appeal that campaign finance reform legislation be enacted by Congress and said he would support a provision to ban foreign nationals from contributing to political parties.
Clinton at first tried to distance himself from the matter, saying the questionable contributions did not go to his re-election campaign, but rather to the general Democratic Party.
But later, he was pressed as to whether he bore some responsibility as titular head of the party. He said party officials were right to return questionable contributions.

"Had that not been done, I would absolutely feel responsible for it," he said. "I'm not trying to declaim responsibility, but I am trying to point out that there is a difference between what the party does and what the (Clinton) campaign does."
